title: An AWS VP shares the 2 biggest AI mistakes he sees in job interviews
summary: AWS VP and distinguished engineer Marc Brooker said that it's "obvious" when someone hasn't kept up with AI developments.
content: Marc Brooker said he sees job seekers make two AI mistakes during interviews. AWS An AWS VP and distinguished engineer said he sees job seekers making two AI mistakes in interviews. The VP, Marc Brooker, said the first mistake is an under-reliance on AI. It's also an issue to over-rely on it, he said, because you offload your thinking. Job seekers want to show they're fluent in AI without suggesting they rely on it too heavily. Communicating that sweet spot can be tricky. Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, said he commonly sees both over- and under-reliance in interviews — and it can be a costly mistake. Brooker said it's increasingly clear when candidates haven't kept pace with how quickly the field has changed over the past year. "It's very obvious when people haven't tried the tools, been building hands-on, been using this new technology, and spending time deeply understanding how it works," Brooker said. He said it can be challenging, even as a leader, to keep up. It can also be difficult to differentiate between a trend and a meaningful update. Identifying that difference requires good taste and a lot of communication with others in the field, Booker said. Personally, he said he dedicates eight hours a week to intentional learning, some of which he does in parallel with building. At least some of this time is set aside for experimenting with new techniques, new tools, papers, and keeping up with the long-term durable trends. This is part of a series of stories from Business Insider's conversation with AWS engineers and executives. To be alerted when the next piece publishes, follow reporter Ana Altchek here. AWS principal engineer says the best engineers are 'paranoid and lazy' when it comes to AI What defines an 'exceptional engineer,' according to the chief AI and technology officer at AWS AWS's Matt Wood has an AI agent help plan his outfit every day The other mistake Booker says he sees is over-relying on the tech. That involves a mindset of, "'I'm just going to ask AI to do this for me,'" or, "'I'm going to hand this question to my agent and answer it.'" Those applicants aren't thinking through answers and design questions. "I want to hire people who can think," Brooker said. "I want to hire people who can deeply consider trade-offs. I want to hire people who can communicate and understand and engage with the technology." Brooker said that simply typing in a problem and then asking an LLM or AI agent to solve it, "isn't a particularly useful or valuable skill." However, the VP said that it's "very useful and valuable" to know when to use AI and when to think for yourself. His comments reflect a growing number of tech leaders who have said that judgment and taste are becoming the most important skills in the field, and that AI is increasingly automating work, leaving engineers with more time for higher-level decision-making. title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed. Past weather incidents have disrupted it before.
summary: In some years, spectators have been injured by falling debris after strong winds sent parade balloons crashing into streetlights.
content: Bad weather has disrupted the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in the past. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed for the first time in history. However, this isn't the first time that bad weather has disrupted the parade. After an incident during the 1997 parade, New York City set new limits on when the balloons could fly. This year's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been pushed to Saturday because of bad weather. It's the first postponement in the event's history, but storms and strong winds have caused trouble before. Over the years, rough conditions have grounded balloons, forced them to fly lower, and sent them crashing into spectators below. Here's a look at how bad weather has disrupted the parade over the years. 1971 Bad weather kept all the balloons on the ground during the 1971 parade. NBC via Getty Images In 1971, strong winds and heavy rain grounded all the parade's giant helium balloons for the only time in its history. The parade floats and performers still made their way down the street, The New York Times reported. 1993 A Sonic the Hedgehog balloon was punctured during the 1993 parade. This photo shows the character at a different year's parade. Charles Norfleet/Getty Images In 1993, strong winds pushed the then-new, 64-foot-tall Sonic the Hedgehog balloon into a streetlamp. The collision punctured the balloon and sent debris falling into the crowd below, injuring a man and a young girl, ABC7NY reported . 1997 The Cat in the Hat balloon struck a light pole during the 1997 parade. Evy Mages/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images In 1997, wind gusts of up to 43 mph damaged several balloons, including Barney and the Pink Panther, the Times reported. The Cat in the Hat balloon also hit a lamppost and snapped off its horizontal metal arm, which fell and struck several spectators below. Police told the Times that one of the victims suffered "very serious" injuries. Following the incidents in 1997, the city introduced new safety rules ahead of the 1998 parade. One barred large balloons from flying if sustained winds exceeded 23 mph or wind gusts exceeded 34 mph. 2005 An M&M balloon hit a lamppost during the 2005 parade, causing a light fixture to fall and injure several spectators. David Handschuh/NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images In 2005, a balloon shaped like a giant M&M collided with a light pole, causing a light fixture to fall onto the crowd below. Two spectators, who are sisters, were left with cuts and bruises, the Times reported. 2019 The balloons flew lower than usual during the 2019 parade because of strong winds. Michael Loccisano/Getty Images In 2019, forecasts of strong winds prompted organizers to lower the balloons from their usual height of 55 feet to right above ground level for safety. title: I quit my corporate job to open a cinnamon roll bakery. A year later, here's what surprised me most.
summary: Arin Senior left corporate finance to open a cinnamon roll bakery in NYC. A year later, she is working 100-hour weeks and but feeling more satisfied.
content: Arin Senior, a financial analyst, left her corporate finance job to open Spirals, a cinnamon-roll bakery in NYC. Eli Nathan/Spirals Arin Senior left her corporate finance job to open a cinnamon-roll bakery in NYC. Senior has never worked in a bakery before and found her scope of work to be surprising. Senior now works 100-hour weeks but would not trade it for her 9-to-5 corporate job. Arin Senior, 26, is the founder of Spirals, a cinnamon-roll bakery in New York City's East Village. She opened the shop in August 2025 after leaving her job as a strategic finance analyst at The Estée Lauder Companies. A Wharton graduate, Senior spent nearly two years developing the idea for Spirals before taking the plunge. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I spent years working in strategy and finance in the corporate beauty industry, but I always knew I wanted to open my own business and be my own boss. Last year, I finally took the leap. I opened Spirals, a cinnamon-bun bakery in New York City , after spending months developing recipes, finding a location, and figuring out everything that goes into starting a business. The day I signed the lease, I quit my corporate job and went all in. We opened in August 2025, and by October, we were profitable. A year into running the bakery, I've learned that being your own boss isn't necessarily about working fewer hours. It's about having more control over what you work on and how you spend your time. My corporate job felt monotonous Spirals, located in New York City's East Village, specializes in cinnamon rolls. Eli Nathan/Spirals My corporate job wasn't bad, but my role was monotonous. I knew exactly what every day would look like. When I was growing up, my dad had his own company, and I loved the lifestyle it gave him. I liked the idea of setting my own schedule and dipping my toe into a whole bunch of different things. I also noticed a gap in New York City's bakery scene . You could find cookies in every flavor, doughnuts, and croissants, but I couldn't find a really great cinnamon roll. I felt there was an opportunity. While still working in finance, I started developing flavors and recipes, researching how to set up an LLC, and looking for a storefront. My husband helped with the search for a space. We looked for about six months before finding the right one. I wanted to be involved in every part of the business. Instead of just evaluating the cost of one product, I could decide what products to launch, how to launch them, and who to market them to. The learning curve was steep Arin Senior has never worked in a bakery before opening Spirals. Eli Nathan/Spirals I'd never run a bakery before. In fact, I'd never even worked in one. The learning curve was steep. There wasn't necessarily one moment when I thought I couldn't do it. There were just a million things to figure out. One of the hardest parts was learning how to delegate. A lot of the strategic decisions start with me. I might decide what we want our menu to look like in June of next year, while my chef takes those ideas and figures out how to execute them. I also handle pricing, marketing, and the broader direction of the business. The biggest lesson I've learned about building a team is that attitude matters more than experience. Hiring and retaining good staff has been by far the hardest part of running the bakery. You can teach people a lot of things, but you can't teach a good attitude. Once I realized that, things got easier. I also had to learn social media from scratch. I'd never posted publicly or edited a video before starting Spirals. I experimented with what people liked, and learned by doing. TikTok initially brought in almost all of our business, alongside influencers who tried our products and posted about them organically. I'm working more hours now Arin Senior said she often works 100 hours a week now as a bakery owner. Eli Nathan/Spirals I think there's a misconception that becoming your own boss means working less. For me, it's actually been the opposite. I'm working 100-hour weeks pretty frequently. There are so many responsibilities I never thought about. The refrigerator breaks, the AC stops working, and suddenly I'm spending time figuring out maintenance issues. But I do have more autonomy over when I work. I can decide to work all day Sunday and take Monday off, or spread a few hours of work across the week. I can fit in a workout class in the middle of the day or travel to see someone on a weekday — things I couldn't have done in my corporate job. I also have a much greater sense of ownership. Almost everything happening at Spirals is something I've had a hand in building. That doesn't mean I never miss aspects of corporate life . I'm occasionally jealous of my husband, who can close his laptop on Friday night and not think about work until Monday. When something goes wrong at a big company, there's usually someone else to turn to. I don't think everyone needs to turn a passionate side project into a storefront in New York City. But having something you love outside your job can still make all the difference. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Mozilla Firefox head says the company is ‘ramping up' the time it devotes to cybersecurity issues
summary: "What we've seen is that we are devoting a lot more of our own resources in order to fix these things," Mozilla's Ajit Varma told Business Insider.
content: Firefox head Ajit Varma said there is still enough time to stay ahead of the AI cybersecurity wave. Alex Broadway/Web Summit via Sportsfile via Getty Images Mozilla's Firefox head says his team has stepped up its efforts to fix cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Ajit Varma said his team is working with both OpenAI and Anthropic. Varma said he still thinks there's "enough time" to fix bugs before the next AI advancements roll out. Mozilla's Firefox chief says the pace of AI advancements is still giving his team "enough time" to make sure it addresses any cybersecurity vulnerabilities. "What we've seen is that we are devoting a lot more of our own resources in order to fix these things," Mozilla's Ajit Varma told Business Insider during a recent interview. "So I think if you look at a year ago, I think it was about 10% of our time, and now, when I look at the latest, it's 27% of our effort is now spent on addressing these." Varma's comments came as top US government officials cautioned that the recent string of outages affecting everything from Microsoft Outlook to JPMorgan Chase reflects companies' efforts to fix software issues faster than ever. Home Depot's chief information officer recently told Business Insider that the retailer wants to cut the time it takes to deploy a fix "to hours." Varma said both OpenAI and Anthropic are giving Mozilla, which is a nonprofit, "a lot of tokens for free." The Firefox head said the frontier models "are finding more and more complicated vulnerabilities within our browser." The AI leaders are eager to work with Mozilla. So much so that Varma said that in March his team noticed that someone with an Anthropic email address had submitted a bug. Since Firefox is completely open source, anyone could do so. Once Mozilla's team got in touch, they realized that the Anthropic employee had found a lot more vulnerabilities. "They were excited about testing their models with Firefox, because we have spent decades building a very secure and very tested browser that's open source, has a lot of contributions and a lot of scrutiny around it," Varma said. Beyond cybersecurity, Varma said, is finding other ways to deploy AI tools to make "Firefox even faster" and prevent issues like memory leaks. He said he encourages his team to view AI as a tool and to "triage" what truly needs human attention. "We are trying to encourage people to say there's a lot of routine activities that we don't necessarily need humans to do and that AI does really well because it's relentless; it doesn't get tired," he said. title: I brought my family to New York for the Thanksgiving Day Parade. It's been on my bucket list since I was a kid, but now I won’t get to see it.
summary: Erin Finney traveled from Florida to NYC with her family to see Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. She can't stay for its Saturday rescheduling.
content: Erin Finney traveled to New York City with her family to see the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, but they will miss its rescheduled Saturday date. Provided by Erin Finney. Erin Finney had always dreamed of seeing the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade live. This year, she brought her family from Florida to New York to check it off her bucket list. They spent about $5,200 on flights and a hotel, but will miss the postponed parade. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Erin Finney, 43, who traveled with her family from Lakeland, Florida, to New York City to catch the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. It has been edited for length and clarity. The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been on my bucket list ever since I was a little girl. I remember going to my grandma’s house, sitting on the floor, and watching it on TV. Even after I got married and had kids, watching the parade was still my tradition. If we went camping for Thanksgiving, I'd still make sure I could catch it. We don't really have a big family back home anymore, and Thanksgiving hasn't felt quite the same. So, this year, I thought we should start doing destination Thanksgivings instead, and check off bucket-list No. 1: seeing the parade in person . I had it all mapped out I traveled to New York with my husband, our three teenage boys, and one of my son's girlfriends. We don't do a whole lot of family vacations with school and work, so this was the first proper one in a while. The boys had been to New York before, but only in the summer. This time, they were going to experience the city in the cold, with all the Christmas decorations up. It was her teenage sons' first time in New York City during the holiday season. Provided by Erin Finney. I spent months planning this trip. There were lots of schedules to rearrange, and I joined a Facebook group to pick up tips and tricks from people who had been to the parade before. We're from Florida, so we don't have a ton of cold-weather stuff. On top of shopping for clothes and making sure everybody had everything they needed, I spent more hours than I'd like to admit mapping out our week, what to do, and where to go. We're staying at a hotel near 48th Street and Sixth Avenue, within walking distance of the parade route. I knew where I was going to sit and had my alarm set for 3:30 a.m. so we could get out there early. I'd read that you couldn't bring chairs, so I bought shower curtains from Dollar Tree for us to sit on. I ordered rain shoes, too, just in case. We spent about $1,500 on flights and about $3,700 on our hotel. As part of the trip, Finney and her husband surprised their sons with tickets to a Giants game. Provided by Erin Finney. We got here on Sunday and went straight to New Jersey to catch a Giants game. It was a surprise for our boys since they play football. We were worried it would get rained out, but it didn't, so I thought the parade would be fine, too. Then came the unexpected news On Wednesday, I was in Brooklyn with my youngest to visit a comic-book store when my oldest son called. I freaked out, thinking somebody was hurt or something was wrong. When he told me the parade had been postponed due to bad weather , I thought he was joking. But then I looked it up, and my stomach dropped. Finney first heard the parade had been postponed through her son and initially thought he was joking. Provided by Erin Finney. I told my family to give me a minute to process what had happened. When I got to the subway, I sat down at the station and started crying. I kept thinking, "Why am I crying?" But I think it was all the excitement leading up to it, and how disappointed I was that I wouldn't get to see the parade after all. We were only meant to be in New York until Friday morning, so we won't be there for the rescheduled parade on Saturday. I looked into changing our flights, but it would have cost at least another $800, plus extra nights at the hotel and food for all of us. I'm also a nurse and am scheduled to work Saturday night, so staying would have meant calling in to work. It just wasn't feasible to extend the trip. The trip was planned around the parade, and Finney was disappointed when it was postponed. Provided by Erin Finney. The parade was the plan, so now we're trying to figure out what to do on Thanksgiving. We hadn't made plans for dinner, but now I'm hoping people might leave early and open up a table somewhere. I understand why the parade was postponed. Safety has to come first, and as a nurse, I would never want anyone to get hurt. I'm disappointed, but the trip has still been great. At the end of the day, it's Thanksgiving, and I'm with my family. I'm thankful for them. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Wall Street wants to understand Gen Z. These high schoolers are giving it a crash course.
summary: High school founders Jasper Gould and Emile Chilingirian have turned their expertise on Gen Z and finance into a 28,000-subscriber newsletter.
content: High school students Emile Chilingirian and Jasper Gould cofounded a finance newsletter. Jasper Gould Jasper Gould cofounded Passing the Torch, a finance and economics newsletter with 28,000 subscribers. The newsletter offers something many others don't: An authentic Gen Z perspective. The newsletter has attracted Wall Street bros as well as young folks interested in finance. Finance analysts sift through heaps of consumer data, conduct large-scale surveys, and meticulously track trends in their quest to understand Gen Z. High school senior Jasper Gould had a better idea. Gould and Emile Chilingirian of New York City cofounded Passing the Torch , a finance and economics newsletter that's amassed 28,000 readers since its official launch in 2025. The newsletter offers an unfiltered glimpse into the minds of Gen Z , the latest generation to drum up spending power. Passing the Torch reports on a wide breadth of topics, from how Zoomers perceive automated vehicles and robotaxis to a deep dive into Pershing Square Capital Management's $65 billion now-defunct takeover bid for Universal Music Group . This month, the duo published an article titled "AI Stocks Just Started Taking Accutane," which discusses the recent tech stock sell-off. Subscribers pay $15 a month, or $150 annually. "We are a proprietary data source of a very special order, and I think people recognize that," Gould, 18, told Business Insider. That's one reason the newsletter has garnered a fan base on Wall Street. "When we looked into the subscriber logs, we saw a concentration at firms like Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan Chase, and Blackstone," Gould said. 'Let's make a business' Although Gould and Chilingirian are now in the media business, they got their start in the nonprofit sector. They cofounded Brooklyn Youth Charitable Investment Group, an organization that teaches financial and leadership skills to high schoolers, in 2024. The nonprofit has 100 active members and over 1,000 students have participated so far. To gain investors, the pair did cold reach-outs while juggling school and their personal lives. "There was a period of time in 10th grade where we were getting three hours of sleep a night, and I'm very happy we were doing so," Gould said. "If you are intentional about your relationships, if you really invest in them, and if you have something going for you like being in high school, that's really all it takes to warm things up." That helped them secure guest speakers from major institutions like Deutsche Bank, the White House, and Apple, Gould said. As the nonprofit grew, Gould and Chilingirian decided to create an Instagram account to share more tips and advice for young folks interested in finance. The account gained over 37,000 followers in less than two years, which inspired Gould and Chilingirian to think bigger. "A lot of the things we're saying are really valuable to investors, so let's make a business," Gould said. They said they didn't have to purchase ads or flood X to find readers. "It was word of mouth, stakeholders in the nonprofit, and people who knew us," Gould said. "In our pursuit of fundraising and working on this organization, we sent a lot of emails, and we had a lot of people in our network." On-the-ground journalism There are certainly challenges to running a media business, including competing in an oversaturated media market and making money amid dwindling online ad rates. There's also the fact that they're still in high school. "The biggest issue is getting people to take us seriously, which generally isn't an issue after the first phone call, but it's always a battle leading into it," Gould said. While the pair conduct traditional research and speak with experts, their youth allows them to take an anthropological approach to tracking Gen Z's tastes. "Just go to a party and ask someone," Gould said. "They don't realize that what they're about to tell us is going to end up making some investor or some company millions of dollars." Although neither founder has graduated from high school yet, they've already envisioned how their brand will continue leveling up. These days, that includes offering their deep insights into Gen Z to companies through consulting. "I'm sure there are some analysts at some of the pod shops that are learning how to read TikTok and Reddit as valuable sources of information, but I'm seeing it in the hallways every day," he said. title: I moved back to Scotland after 19 years in the US. Thanksgiving is the one tradition I refuse to give up.
summary: After 19 years in the US, I brought Thanksgiving home to Scotland. Celebrating it abroad has become an important family tradition.
content: The author moved back to Scotland in 2020 but still celebrates Thanksgiving. Courtesy of the author I moved to the US in 2001 knowing nothing about Thanksgiving, but it quickly became a holiday I loved. Since moving back to Scotland in 2020, I've kept celebrating Thanksgiving despite a few challenges. Celebrating Thanksgiving in Scotland feels strange, but it keeps me connected to my life in the US. When I moved to the US to study abroad in 2001, I was baffled by the traditions of Thanksgiving. As the years went by, however, I developed a real appreciation for this American holiday — even if I've never quite been able to wrap my head around adding marshmallows to sweet potato. In my early years in the US, I attended Thanksgiving dinners because everyone around me did. Over time, though, I grew to love the simplicity of the holiday — so much so that I brought the tradition home with me when I returned to the UK after 19 years. It's a holiday about gratitude, not gifts I love that there's no pressure around buying gifts or religious ceremony — Thanksgiving is about spending time with people I love, being community-minded, and giving thanks for the small things in life. In Colorado, I'd host friends who didn't have family nearby Courtesy of the author When I lived in the US, I ran in the local Turkey Trot to raise money for charity every Thanksgiving morning, and taught a special gratitude-themed yoga class afterwards. I hosted dinners for friends who also didn't have family nearby and learned to make my own cranberry sauce, adding some dishes from Scotland, like my mom's leeks in cheese sauce. My homemade pumpkin cheesecake became an annual request. When I moved back to Scotland after nearly two decades in the US, I didn't expect that an American holiday would become one of the things that helped me feel at home again . It helped me with a major life transition My first year back in Scotland was a whirlwind of finding a job, a new home, and establishing new routines. Once things settled down, though, I realized how much I missed having an annual occasion to celebrate the good things in life. While my friends in the US were readying their turkey dinners or making plans to fly home and be with family, here in Scotland, life just carried on as normal. The days were getting shorter and colder, and I was in desperate need of some festive cheer to warm my spirits. It was my partner who suggested we celebrate Thanksgiving. Courtesy of the author It was my English partner who suggested we host our own Thanksgiving meal in Scotland. He had a friend from the US who was always homesick at this time of year, and we thought his two kids would relish the opportunity to experience an American holiday that they've only seen in movies. It's strange celebrating a holiday when the rest of the country goes to work My partner volunteered to take on the turkey, and I made a shopping list for the rest. Getting the basics was pretty easy, but some items weren't so readily available. After a half day of searching, I finally found canned pumpkin at a local health food store (at nearly $5 a can), and my American friend saved the day with a bag of fresh cranberries. Our teenager even took a break from his Rubik's Cube to peel sprouts, but it didn't last long Courtesy of the author It felt a bit strange celebrating a holiday when the rest of the country was at work. The kids went to school, I had to prep the meal between work tasks, and there would be no day off on Friday to recover. After school, the day took on an atmosphere of excitement, however. The kids enjoyed the novelty of a holiday their school friends weren't celebrating, and my stepson even put down his Rubik's Cube for 20 minutes to help prepare the sprouts. A few friends crowded into our kitchen, and we managed to find the football game on satellite television, although I don't think anyone understood the rules. Our first Thanksgiving was quite traditional, with all the classics Courtesy of the author Once dinner was ready, taking turns to say what we were grateful for felt unfamiliar to some of my guests, but everyone joined in. The funniest part was seeing my friends' faces when our American friend presented his sweet potatoes with marshmallows. At times, everyone looked as bewildered as I felt on my first Thanksgiving, but it turned out to be a tradition that can easily translate across cultures. For most other people in Scotland, it was just an average Thursday night, but for the first time in a year, I felt really connected to the life I'd left behind. Living abroad taught me that home isn't just where you come from Since 2021, we've found a way to honor Thanksgiving almost every year. Sometimes it's just a quiet dinner with my partner and his daughter; last year, it coincided with a visit from our Swedish friends, and we ended up with a large group crammed into my tiny apartment . Last year it coincided with a visit from our Swedish friends, so we all crammed into my tiny apartment Courtesy of the author I've found that people from all over the world are really interested in the ideas behind Thanksgiving, and are usually thrilled to be invited over. I can't believe that a can of pumpkin puree here costs more than a gallon of gas in the US, and I still haven't found a reliable source of fresh cranberries. But I've learned handy substitutes, like using butternut squash or sweet potato puree for pumpkin, and red currants or sour cherries for cranberries. Scotland may be where I grew up, but moving back after 19 years wasn't quite as simple as I expected. I left friends, routines, and the life I'd built behind. Keeping Thanksgiving alive has helped me hold on to that part of myself while making a new life here. Next year, I want to organize my own mini Turkey Trot before dinner — even if we all have to get up early and fit it in before work. It's one more American tradition I can make my own, wherever home happens to be. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I’m a Silicon Valley couples therapist. Here’s what Jensen Huang's daily therapy sessions might entail.
summary: Here's what Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's daily therapy sessions might include, according to a Silicon Valley therapist who treats high-profile couples.
content: Phil Boissierie has been a couples' therapist in Silicon Valley for almost 20 years. Courtesy of Phil Boissierie At an Nvidia all-hands, reinstated CEO Jensen Huang said he'll be in therapy for 90 minutes a day. Phil Boissierie is a Silicon Valley therapist who works with couples in high-profile careers. He hasn't met Huang but says therapy could include managing public pressure and relationship repair. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Phil Boissierie, a 50-year-old marriage and couples therapist at The Relationship Therapy Group in Silicon Valley. His words have been edited for length and clarity. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently said he was doing 90 minutes of therapy every day as part of his effort to move forward. I've been a couples therapist in Silicon Valley for 20 years. Ninety minutes of therapy a day is not particularly common, nor is it a traditional model. Usually, if someone's doing that much therapy every day, it's because they're likely trying to work through a lot quickly and create some behavioral change. If a behavior is compulsive or hard to change, doing extended periods of therapy every day can be helpful for building traction. I can't say for sure what he's doing since I don't know Jensen, but here's what that frequency of therapy for a high-profile CEO in a situation like this would probably look like. There will be a lot to work through Working through how to manage public pressure, understand repetitive behavior, and repair relationships are all things I would discuss in the first few sessions of intensive therapy like this. The pressure, the eyes on him , the eyes on the company — all of that is huge, alongside all the damage that's been created in his relationships with his wife, his family, and the other people he's been involved with and working with. Do you think Jensen Huang should have been reinstated? Take our survey . Any therapy plan has to do with what the particular person is going through, and I'm not going to speculate, but in my practice, a lot of times when we see someone having multiple affairs , that doesn't just come out of nowhere. It often has to do with family of origin, early life experiences, and things they're working through, which become the fabric of who we are and how we operate. It takes intentional work to create those changes. I also always recommend to people that when a disclosure comes out about an affair, doing work as a couple right up front is really important. If Jensen and Lori Huang are also doing couples work, I think that would be really, really smart and not overkill. The 90-minute frequency, every day, helps you get through a lot In a traditional 50-minute therapy session, it's common for people to settle into things, then, right as they're doing some heavy lifting and reaching an insight that's particularly challenging or emotional, the session's over. So, by allowing 90 minutes, you're able to settle in and cover a lot more. Working every day in therapy like this could help him pick right back up where they left off the day before, not only face what's happening that day, what's coming up, and all the pressures, but also get a jumpstart on that intensive work of answering questions like, "Why did this happen? How do I stop this from happening again?" Hopefully, that would be a big part of his motivation for doing this much therapy. This also signals something to his company and to people watching Sometimes coming back into the workplace after such a big public situation requires satisfying people. I think that could also be a part of this. It demonstrates to those watching that someone is working hard on themselves. If multiple affairs are happening, if that is what's happening here, it's easy for people to say, "Look, if you're involved in all of this, how are you paying attention to what's going on at the company?" I would imagine if he came out and said, "Hey, I'm going to do an hour a week of therapy, or I'm going to do two hours a week," that just wouldn't suffice for people. If you're going to make the behavioral change, repair the relationships, and take the helm of the company , yeah, you do have to make changes all over the place to be healthy again. Do you have a story to share about your relationship affecting your career? If so, please reach out to the reporter at aapplegate@businessinsider.com . Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade postponed for the first time in its history
summary: Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade has been postponed due to weather. The annual event is now set for Saturday at 8:30 a.m.
content: Workers deflate balloons on Wednesday night after the parade was postponed to Saturday. Adam Gray/Getty Images Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed to Saturday due to weather. It's the parade's first postponement and the first time it won't march on Thanksgiving since WWII. Over 3.5 million people attend the parade in New York City each year. Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade has been postponed, disrupting the holiday plans of more than 3.5 million people who typically attend the annual event. The parade is now set for 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, according to a statement from the company, which said the rescheduling was due to weather. A storm forecast to bring strong winds and moderate to heavy rainfall is projected to hit the East Coast during the holiday, according to the National Weather Service in New York. At a press conference on Wednesday evening, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, "I know that many New Yorkers, myself included, as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," standing in front of a star-shaped Macy's balloon. "Generation after generation has watched SpongeBob and Spider-Man soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down Sixth Avenue," Mamdani added. "I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first." The planned balloon viewing went ahead on Wednesday. Julie Zeveloff Will Coss, vice president and head of Macy's Studios, said at the press conference that the company was "heartbroken" by the postponement, adding that "this parade has been built with love." Macy's said in a statement last year that the parade, which began in New York City in 1924, would make its 100th march in 2026. This is the first time the event has been postponed in its history, and the first time since World War II that the parade will not take place on Thanksgiving , when it was canceled in 1942, 1943, and 1944, as materials that would've been used were diverted to the war effort. The storm has also disrupted a parade in Philadelphia, which calls itself the oldest Thanksgiving parade in the US. Unlike the Macy's parade, the 6abc Dunkin' Thanksgiving Day Parade won't be rescheduled. Instead, it will be a TV-only event that will take place on Thanksgiving morning. Workers deflate a giant Shrek balloon. Adam Gray/Getty Images In New York, images showed workers deflating iconic balloons including Mickey Mouse, Shrek, and Buzz Lightyear on Wednesday night after the postponement was announced. The postponement has left a wave of people, including tourists and parade performers, scrambling to make last-minute accommodations. Pearland High School's 500-member band is among the groups scrambling to change plans. The Texas district said keeping students in New York through Saturday could add nearly $400,000 in unplanned hotel and flight costs, and it launched a donation drive to help cover them. The disruption has also upset visitors who booked a Thanksgiving-only trip to see the milestone 100th parade. On social media, visitors said that they planned to have reunions around the parade, with family flying in from different parts of the country. Some tourists said they are paying premium prices to rebook flights and hotels, while others said their bucket-list trips would remain unfulfilled because they find it unaffordable to extend their stays. Erin Finney, who traveled with her family from Lakeland, Florida, to New York City to catch the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, said that it had been on her bucket list since she was a child. "When I got to the subway, I sat down at the station and started crying. I kept thinking, "Why am I crying?" But I think it was all the excitement leading up to it, and how disappointed I was that I wouldn't get to see the parade after all," she told Business Insider. She added, "I looked into changing our flights, but it would have cost at least another $800, plus extra nights at the hotel and food for all of us." Amanda Goh contributed reporting. title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel as more than 6,000 flights are delayed
summary: Coastal flooding, strong winds, and heavy rainfall are expected to batter the East Coast this Thanksgiving.
content: A storm is headed toward the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day. Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images Storms are disrupting travel ahead of Thanksgiving. More than 6,500 US flights were delayed on Wednesday, according to FlightAware. A storm expected to bring strong winds and coastal flooding to the East Coast has forced the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to be postponed. Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel, with more severe weather expected to hit the East Coast on Thursday. More than 6,500 flights within, into, or out of the US were delayed on Wednesday, and about 160 were canceled, according to FlightAware. As of about 1:30 a.m. ET Thursday, roughly 120 flights had been delayed and 300 canceled. The National Weather Service wrote in a Wednesday report that the East Coast can expect "major coastal flooding, beach erosion, strong wind gusts, and heavy rainfall" during Thanksgiving. Scattered power outages and tree damage are also likely, it added. A map from the weather service showed winter, gale, coastal flood, and wind warnings along the country's eastern coast. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Wednesday X post that New Yorkers should expect severe weather on Thursday, including winds up to 60 miles per hour. He said that, to protect New Yorkers, the city, along with Macy's and the local police department, had decided to postpone the 100th Annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday. This is the first time in history that the iconic parade has been rescheduled. "The worst of the storm is expected to hit on Thanksgiving Day in the afternoon through the late evening," he added in his X post. He provided a list of steps New Yorkers should take to protect themselves ahead of the storm, such as staying indoors, moving cars away from coastal areas to higher ground, and budgeting extra time for travel. The Transportation Security Administration said in a Saturday X post that it expects to screen nearly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between November 24 and November 30, including more than 3 million on Sunday, November 29. It recommended that travelers arrive early for their flights. The Federal Aviation Administration wrote in a Wednesday X post that gusty winds may slow flights at LaGuardia Airport, Newark Liberty Airport, JFK, and San Francisco International Airport that day. It added that thunderstorms may cause delays at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. title: Thomson Reuters is using both American and Chinese AI for its next model
summary: Thomson Reuters blends Google's Gemma and Z.ai's GLM to build Thomson 1.1, hoping to cut AI costs by using both Chinese and US open-source models.
content: Thomson Reuters CEO Steve Hasker. John Lamparski/Getty Images for Advertising Week New York Forget the AI race: Thomson Reuters wants the best of both worlds. The company's next AI model is built off Google's Gemma and Z.ai's GLM, it tells Business Insider. The data and legal giant has spent $40 million so far building its own chatbots. As China and the US race to compete on AI, Thomson Reuters, the Canadian data and legal giant, is having it both ways. The company is launching a new AI model called Thomson 1.1 by the end of the year, it tells Business Insider exclusively — and it's built on open-source models from both countries: China's GLM, from Z.ai, and Google's Gemma. By using open-source models that anyone can download and host, Thomson Reuters hopes to reduce its AI costs and take more control over its intellectual property. There's a battle in tech over which AI corporations will use. It pits cheaper Chinese open-source models against closed ones from giants like Anthropic and OpenAI. US companies like Google, Meta, and Thinking Machines Lab have also released powerful open-source models in recent months. It's a shift for Thomson Reuters , which didn't use American AI for its previous in-house model, Thomson 1.0. Instead, it built its chatbot off Qwen, an AI from the Chinese tech giant Alibaba. "The US government, and many other governments around the world, prefer to have US and Western sovereign models at the foundation of what we do," Thomson Reuters' chief technology officer, Joel Hron, told Business Insider. "Where we can, we're going to use Western and US-based labs to ground Thomson." Hron said the company still uses Z.ai's GLM because it excels at using computers — a key feature of AI agents . It also chose Google's Gemma because of its small size and efficiency, he added. Thomson Reuters aims to build an AI that helps its clients with mid-tier work, such as tax advice. For the most difficult tasks, it still plans to use OpenAI and Anthropic. "There's a lot of work that happens in the middle, and that's where we get real economic benefit," Hron said. Open source has its limitations It takes a lot of money for a big company to build a custom AI chatbot, even if it uses free, open-source models. Hron told Business Insider that so far, Thomson Reuters has spent about $40 million on the effort to tweak and tune its own models. That money goes to things like chips, data, and salaries for AI researchers. Adoption is early. Less than 5% of all AI tokens used at Thomson Reuters come from its own AI, Hron said — although that is set to ramp up in the coming years as its focus areas expand. Chinese models also have built-in censorship features that can be tricky to unwind. Hirundo, a startup in Israel, sent Business Insider an analysis showing that one version of the current Thomson model parrots Chinese government talking points. For example, it refused to acknowledge the Tiananmen Square massacre and said that "Taiwan is an inalienable part of China." A Thomson Reuters spokesperson said that its AI handles such questions "substantially better" when it's used as intended — with a set of instructions to follow. The company's coming AI model further reduces bias, the spokesperson added. To large companies hit by high token bills — like Pinterest , AT&T, and others — the appeal of open source remains strong: it can reduce recurring AI costs and give companies technology they own and control. "Thomson is what AI sovereignty actually looks like in practice," Andrew Bean, Thomson Reuters' lead AI scientist, said. Read the original article on Business Insider
